title: Plain silk, uncarved wood
hook: show plainness, embrace simplicity, have few desires (Tao Te Ching 19)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was when the way is lost: rules about kindness come after the way goes missing. Your line was before the rule.

Two pieces of wood on a workbench. One is a finished carving: a bird, every feather cut in, polished, perfect. The other is a plain block, straight from the tree, nothing done to it yet. Which one could still become anything? The bird is beautiful, and it will only ever be a bird. The block could be a bowl, a spoon, a bird, a handle, a toy. Chapter nineteen of the Tao Te Ching reaches for that block. Its name for it is a single word, pu.
screen: `A FINISHED CARVING.` → `A PLAIN BLOCK.` → `WHICH COULD STILL BECOME ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: First, the chapter starts by throwing things out. Give up sageliness and cleverness, it says, and the people will be better off. Give up kindness and righteousness, and the people will return to devotion and care in their families. Give up craftiness and profit, and there'll be no thieves. It picks up where yesterday left off: the named virtues came after the way was lost, so let the names go. Second, it admits that's not enough. Throwing things out leaves a hole, and people need something to hold on to. So it offers three things: show plainness, embrace the uncarved, be less selfish and want less. Third, the two pictures. Plainness here is su, raw silk, undyed, the cloth before anyone colors it. The uncarved is pu, wood in the block, before anyone shapes it. Both are materials in their first state: not poor, not ugly, just not yet worked over. A person, like silk or wood, can be dyed and carved by praise, ambition, cleverness and wanting, until there's no room left to become anything else. Fourth, what it isn't. Pu isn't a call to be simple-minded. Some readers hear an invitation to stay a little unfinished, to keep some of yourself raw and plain, with room to grow in a new direction. The carving is admired. The block is free.
screen: `GIVE UP CLEVERNESS AND THE NAMED VIRTUES.` · `PEOPLE NEED SOMETHING TO HOLD.` · `RAW SILK, UNCARVED WOOD.` · `STAY A LITTLE UNFINISHED.` · then, large: `EMBRACE THE UNCARVED.`

segments.voice: Rest your eyes on one plain thing near you, a cotton shirt, a wooden spoon, a white mug, a glass of water, and notice it as it is, with nothing added: its weight, its color, its texture. Then turn the same attention to yourself, the part of you before titles and opinions and plans: not better, not worse, just plain and uncarved.
Pu. Uncarved wood, the block before anyone shapes it: chapter nineteen's picture of a person not yet worked over. Today's word.
Your line: uncarved. The block can still become a bowl, a spoon or a bird. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take pu, the uncarved block, as a reason to keep their lives and belongings plain, and to leave room in themselves for what isn't finished yet.

chat.says: Why would the Tao Te Ching praise a plain block of wood?
options: The uncarved block can still become anything; some read pu as room to grow.
Because plain wood was the costliest treasure in old China.
Because it says the wise should never change or grow at all.
chat.meaning: Chapter nineteen offers pu, wood in the block before anyone shapes it: not poor or simple-minded, but still able to become something new.

pu.meaning: uncarved wood, the block before anyone shapes it

notes: Chapter 19 paraphrased throughout. The chapter's 'a hundredfold' benefit was left out under the claims rule.

'Give up kindness and righteousness as slogans' adds 'as slogans', an interpretive gloss that links to chapter 18; the Guodian version reads differently here. A scholar should check whether the gloss is fair.
'Pu shows up again later in the Tao Te Ching' (e.g. chapters 28, 32, 37) is a claim about the text; 'some readers count it among the book's central images' is attributed. Confirm.
Glosses: 素 (sù) raw or undyed silk; 樸 (pǔ) uncarved wood, the raw block. Confirm.
The bird carving illustration is the writer's, not the text's.
